newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle flies satellite on robot arm.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle flies satellite on robot arm.

text.p: The five-member crew of the shuttle Columbia sent a prototype semiconductor factory into space for a second time on Tuesday, but this time kept it tethered to the spacecraft's robot arm on its journey around Earth.
Astronaut Tom Jones extended Columbia's robot arm, which was to hold the Wake Shield Facility for a period of more than six hours, during which it was to travel through space attached to the shuttle.

Wake Shield, a prototype disk-shaped satellite that produces very thin films for use in advanced semiconductors for the electronics industry, was to make oxide chips from oxygen encountered during its trip through low-earth orbit.

The satellite was scheduled to return to Columbia's cargo bay early on Wednesday morning. Tuesday night's operation was to have taken about three hours, but NASA decided to allow the project more time. Administrators said the change would not affect the timing of the astronauts' other activities.

On Monday night Jones had used Columbia's robot arm to snatch the Wake Shield from space after shuttle commander Ken Cockrell manoeuvred the orbiter around and beneath the free-floating satellite in a complicated operation that NASA managers and Columbia's crew said had gone very well.
"I think it's (the mission) going pretty much by the book, and that's a good thing," Cockrell told NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin in a telephone conversation.

The retrieval on Monday was made more complicated by a second satellite also released from Columbia, the Orfeus-Spas telescope, travelling nearby. But the two multi-million dollar satellites remained a safe distance apart, NASA officials said.

To help keep Orfeus-Spas from straying too close to the Wake Shield, the observatory's scientific operations were stopped for several hours. NASA administrators would not say on Tuesday whether they were considering extending Columbia's 16-day mission to make up for that lost time.
"We don't have any word on that at this time," a spokeswoman said.
The orbiter is now scheduled for landing Dec. 5 at 7:40 a.m. EST (1240 GMT) at the Kennedy Space Centre.
During his call Goldin asked the astronauts if they would like to remain in space for an extra day. "You read my mind, sir. We've got quite a bit more work to do," Cockrell said.
The astronauts also were to lower the pressure in Columbia's cabin early on Wednesday in preparation for a spacewalk on Thursday, the first of two during the mission.
The Orfeus-Spas continued to trail behind Columbia. The shuttle was scheduled to retrieve that satellite on Dec. 3.
